lead: Zone 2 cardio is low-to-moderate intensity steady aerobic exercise, the second band in popular five-zone heart-rate schemes, often described as a pace at which conversation is still possible. It is used by people who want to lean out and improve conditioning without the fatigue of hard intervals: easy sessions of walking, cycling, rowing, swimming or jogging burn calories, lean on fat as the main fuel and leave energy for lifting, so they can be added to a physique plan without eating into recovery.[1]

Wikipedia's aerobic exercise article describes repeated light-to-moderate activity over extended periods, with fat and glycogen as the main fuels and relatively more fat used at lower intensity.[1] Endurance training also drives mitochondrial biogenesis, in which energy depletion activates AMPK and the regulator PGC-1 alpha, raising the muscle's oxidative capacity over time.[2]

The 'Zone 2' name has no single standard definition: heart-rate zones can be built from a percentage of maximum heart rate, from heart rate reserve (the Karvonen method) or from fixed offsets below maximum (the Zoladz method).[3] No published trial has tested Zone 2 as a named protocol for appearance.

chain: Calories burned with fat as a main fuel and low recovery cost
Added to a deficit alongside lifting
Lower body fat and better conditioning
angle.text: Zone 2 sessions add energy expenditure and aerobic fitness at an intensity easy enough to sit alongside weight training. Over weeks they support a leaner look and better work capacity for training.

infobox: Brisk walking, easy cycling, swimming, jogging[1]
Conversational pace; heart-rate zone defined several ways[3]

paras: Aerobic exercise guidance recommends about 2.5 hours a week of moderate activity to lower health risks, and even about 11 minutes a day has been associated with lower risk of early death, with high-intensity interval training possibly giving similar benefits in less time.[1]

Training intensity can be written as a percentage of maximum heart rate. Wikipedia notes that the common 220-minus-age estimate was not derived from original research and can be off by about 24 beats per minute for an individual at the 95 percent level, so zones set from it are approximate; a supervised maximal test is the most accurate method.[3] Under the Zoladz method, zones are set from maximum heart rate minus fixed adjusters, with zone 1 for a maximum of 180 about 125 to 135 beats per minute.[3]

Zone models differ between watches, apps, coaches and indoor-bike software, so 'Zone 2' can mean different heart-rate ranges or wattages. Laboratory descriptions are tied to lactate rather than to fixed heart-rate zones: Wikipedia's endurance-training page describes 'extensive basic endurance' work as lactate clearly below the aerobic threshold, at about 50 to 77 percent, for sessions of one to eight hours, while 'intensive' steady work goes up toward the anaerobic threshold at 77 to 85 percent.[4]

The lactate threshold is the intensity at which blood lactate begins to rise rapidly, given there as roughly 85 percent of maximum heart rate or 75 percent of maximum oxygen uptake. The aerobic threshold, where lactate first rises above resting levels, is placed at about 65 to 85 percent of maximum heart rate and near 2 mmol/L. The term 'zone 2' is not used in that article; its closest equivalent is the volume below the first lactate turning point (LT1).[5] Polarized training, derived from observation of elite endurance athletes, allocates about 80 percent of weekly training volume below LT1 and a smaller share above the second threshold.[5]
Many lifters rely on a simpler proxy, the talk test: an intensity at which full sentences are still possible.

At lower intensities the body relies mainly on fat, shifting toward glycogen as intensity rises; the same source notes that low-to-moderate exercise burns fewer calories per unit time than high-intensity exercise.[1] A training table on Wikipedia's endurance training page lists 'extensive basic endurance' sessions as aimed at health, endurance and fat metabolism.[4]

Long-term endurance training is described as lowering resting heart rate and raising stroke volume and cardiac output, raising the oxidative enzyme succinate dehydrogenase about 2.5-fold and myoglobin by 75 to 80 percent in well-trained athletes.[4] Endurance exercise also stimulates mitochondrial biogenesis through AMPK and PGC-1 alpha signalling, increasing the muscle's oxidative capacity.[2]

The term in its current popular sense is closely associated with physiologist Iñigo San Millán, who has worked with elite cyclists and, with physician Peter Attia, discussed it on the Peter Attia Drive podcast in episodes released in 2019 and 2022.[9] In the episode summary, San Millán says Zone 2 is where, over 25 years of working with athletes, he has seen the biggest improvement in fat burning, which he links to improvements in mitochondrial function.[9] The same page describes a Zone 2 protocol used both to test and to improve mitochondrial function, and Attia's site defines Zone 2 as the highest metabolic output a person can sustain while keeping blood lactate below about 2 millimoles per litre.[9]

That lactate-based definition differs from the heart-rate bands in consumer watches and apps, which is why the number of the zone does not map to the same effort in every system.[9][3] San Millán divides training into six zones, and the episodes discuss the boundary between Zone 2 and Zone 3.[9]

sections.h: Use in physique and looksmaxxing communities
paras: Zone 2 sessions are discussed as a way to add cardio during a cut without hard intervals, and as a way to build the aerobic base that supports faster recovery between sets. Strength-training logs on forums such as T Nation commonly mention easy cardio alongside lifting, for example incline treadmill walks logged with calories during a diet phase,[6] Peloton rides written up by zone, and interval sessions that alternate harder zones with brief zone 2 recoveries.[7][8]
The chain people describe is that easy sessions add weekly energy expenditure with little extra fatigue, which supports fat loss alongside resistance training and keeps a lean, conditioned look.

Wikipedia's endurance training article notes that endurance exercise can lower testosterone levels and that very high-volume endurance training, mainly in extreme events, has been linked to adverse cardiac remodelling; it also notes that short-term strength training has been found beneficial for endurance performance, so the two can be combined.[4]

No studies found specific to Zone 2 as a named protocol. General evidence on aerobic exercise is summarised under its own topic,[1] and lactate-threshold physiology and polarized training are described in encyclopedia sources.[5]

Studies comparing training intensities for body composition give the closest related evidence. A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis by Wewege and colleagues in Obesity Reviews pooled 13 trials in overweight and obese adults, with training lasting about ten weeks at three sessions a week. Both high-intensity interval training and moderate-intensity continuous training significantly reduced whole-body fat mass and waist circumference, the two did not differ significantly on any body-composition measure, and interval training needed about 40 percent less training time.[10] Those trials used moderate-intensity continuous exercise as a comparison rather than a lactate-defined Zone 2 protocol, so they describe the wider category of steady aerobic work.

lore.intro: On T Nation, training logs mention easy cardio, zone-labelled bike rides and walks around lifting and dieting, with Zone 2 treated as one setting among several rather than a stand-alone system.[6][7][8]

claims.claim: Easy cardio can be added during a cut without hurting lifting.
claims.believers: Users log incline treadmill walks and similar easy sessions during diet phases alongside weight training.[6]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes lower-intensity exercise as relying mainly on fat for fuel but burning fewer calories per unit time than high-intensity exercise; no published trial has tested Zone 2 as a named protocol for body composition.[1]

claims.claim: Short zone 2 blocks serve as recovery between hard intervals.
claims.believers: Peloton and bike logs describe alternating zone 3, 4 or 5 efforts with brief zone 2 or zone 1 recoveries.[7][8]
claims.experts: Endurance-training references list recovery sessions with lactate below the aerobic threshold as a standard category of training.[4]

claims.claim: Zone numbers are comparable between devices and people.
claims.believers: Logs quote zone numbers (for example a seven-zone bike scheme where the user mostly uses about five) as if shared.[7]
claims.experts: Heart-rate zones can be built from percentage of maximum, heart rate reserve or fixed offsets, and the 220-minus-age formula can be off by about 24 beats per minute for an individual.[3]

name: Zone 2 cardio

card.summary: Easy, steady cardio at conversational pace; popular, but little zone-specific research for appearance goals.
card.note: No trials of Zone 2 as such have been published.

quick.overview:
Zone 2 is steady, easy-to-moderate cardio, usually measured by heart rate or the ability to talk.
It is widely promoted for fat use and endurance, but no trials of Zone 2 as a named method have been published.
quick.mechanism: Low intensity relies mostly on fat for fuel, with more glycogen used as intensity rises.
quick.risks: General aerobic exercise is considered low-risk; people with health conditions are generally advised to consult a clinician.
